summary: Allows DNSSEC-validating resolvers to use NSEC and NSEC3 records from cache to generate negative answers for whole ranges of names, and positive answers from wildcards. This can improve speed, reduce load, and increase privacy. It updates RFC 4035 and is updated by RFC 9077.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking again whether a name exists, a resolver uses its notes that nothing lives between two names, and answers right away.

questions: how does dnssec negative caching work
what is the maximum negative cache ttl
subtitle: Let validating DNS resolvers answer 'no such name' for a whole range of names from one cached proof.

tldr.problem: A DNS negative cache needs an exact match, so a resolver that learned cat.example.com does not exist still asks the servers again about dog.example.com, wasting bandwidth, adding delay and leaking queries.
tldr.mechanism: A validating resolver keeps validated NSEC/NSEC3 records and uses the range each one covers to answer later queries inside that range straight from cache. It can also build positive answers from a cached wildcard.
tldr.outcome: Answers come faster and authoritative servers see fewer queries. RFC 8198 updates RFC 4035 and is itself updated by RFC 9077.

today: RFC 8198 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 4035. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9077.

sections.title: Why Exact-Match Negative Caching Falls Short
sections.content:
The DNS relies on caching to scale, but a lookup in the negative cache (the cache of facts such as 'this RRset does not exist') needs an exact match. That leads to extra lookups, higher latency, extra work on both authoritative and recursive servers, and less privacy because queries leak out.

RFC 8198 updates RFC 4035 so that a DNSSEC-validating resolver can use NSEC and NSEC3 records already in its cache to synthesize negative answers. It also allows positive answers to be synthesized when a wildcard record is involved. The idea was first proposed in Section 6 of RFC 5074 (DNSSEC Lookaside Validation).
sections.eli5: Normally the resolver only remembers the exact names it was told do not exist. This document lets it remember whole gaps of names instead.

sections.title: The Problem in Two Examples
sections.content:
Take a signed example.com zone holding albatross, elephant and zebra. A query for cat.example.com returns an NSEC record saying nothing exists alphabetically between albatross and elephant (or an NSEC3 record saying nothing exists between two hashed names). The resolver learns that cat does not exist, but it ignores that the proof covers a whole range. A later query for ball.example.com or dog.example.com goes out to the servers again.

The RFC lists the costs: wasted bandwidth, state kept on the recursive server for outstanding queries, extra questions for the authoritative server, longer waits for the user, a path for attackers to cause a denial of service, and privacy leaks such as typos travelling further than needed.

The second example is a zone with avocado, a wildcard *.example.org and zucchini. After leek.example.org is answered from the wildcard, a query for banana.example.org still goes out even though the resolver already has proof that the wildcard applies.
sections.eli5: It is like phoning the library every time you want a book that is not there, even after they already told you nothing is shelved between A and E.

sections.title: How the Cache Is Used Aggressively
sections.content:
If the negative cache has enough information to validate the query, the resolver SHOULD use NSEC, NSEC3 and wildcard records to synthesize the answer. Otherwise it MUST fall back to sending the query to the authoritative servers.

With NSEC, the resolver checks that cached records cover the query name and match or cover the source of synthesis. If denial of existence follows the rules in Section 5.4 of RFC 4035, it returns NXDOMAIN or NODATA immediately. NSEC3 is harder, because the resolver must also check empty non-terminals and wildcards derived from the query name, using Sections 8.4 to 8.7 of RFC 5155. If a covering NSEC3 record has the Opt-Out flag, it does not prove the name is absent and aggressive caching is not possible for that name.

For wildcards, as long as the resolver can determine that the name would not exist without the wildcard match, it SHOULD synthesize an answer (or a NODATA response) from the cache-deduced wildcard. If the wildcard record is not in the cache, it MUST ask the authoritative servers.
sections.eli5: If the resolver has a signed note that covers the gap your name falls into, it answers from the note. If the note is missing or does not prove enough, it asks the real server.

sections.title: Relaxing RFC 4035 and Limiting TTLs
sections.content:
Section 4.5 of RFC 4035 advised resolvers not to use wildcards or NSEC records to produce answers on their own, so that they would not block new authoritative data. RFC 8198 argues this can be relaxed. Without the technique, an exact-name lookup could already have cached a negative answer, so zone operators should not expect a newly added name to work immediately anyway.

The paragraph is replaced with this rule: once the records are validated, validating resolvers SHOULD use wildcards and NSEC/NSEC3 records to generate positive and negative responses until the effective TTLs or signatures expire.

Because newly added names cannot be used while negative information is effective, TTLs matter. Validating resolvers are RECOMMENDED to cap the effective TTL of negative responses at 10800 seconds (3 hours), the default maximum in RFC 2308. A resolver SHOULD also reduce the TTL of NSEC/NSEC3 records to SOA.MINIMUM from the negative response when that is smaller.
sections.eli5: The old rule said do not trust your notes, in case the phone book changed. The new rule says trust them until they expire, and never keep them longer than three hours.

sections.title: Benefits
sections.content:
The RFC names three direct gains. Latency drops because the resolver can tell clients immediately that a name does not exist. Recursive servers do less work because they send fewer queries and keep less state. Authoritative servers receive fewer queries, which saves bandwidth, queries per second and CPU.

The size of the benefit depends on the query distribution. The text says that, at the time of writing, around 65% of queries to root name servers result in NXDOMAIN, and this technique will eliminate a sizable quantity of them.

It may also help against random-QNAME attacks, where attackers query many random subdomains. It will not always work as a defense, not least because not many zones are DNSSEC signed at all. The authors also hope that these benefits, which only accrue to DNSSEC users, will encourage more DNSSEC deployment.
sections.eli5: Fewer phone calls means quicker answers for you and less work for the people answering the phone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using NSEC/NSEC3 records without DNSSEC validation may create serious security issues, so the technique requires validation.

Newly registered records may not be usable at once, but choosing a suitable TTL and negative-cache TTL (SOA.MINIMUM) mitigates this, and the RFC says it is not a security problem. Capping the maximum TTL of cached NSEC/NSEC3 records, for example at 10800 seconds, also helps.

One risk is cache poisoning. A record's TTL is typically minutes or hours, but its RRSIG expiry can be weeks away. An attacker who spoofs responses might plant old NSEC/NSEC3 records. Without aggressive use the attacker must repeat the attack for every query. With it, one success can suppress many queries for new names, up to the negative TTL.
sections.eli5: Notes are only safe if they are signed, and a forged old note could fool the resolver for a while, so notes should not be kept for too long.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Cached negative answers used to be indexed by QNAME, QCLASS, QTYPE and the CD bit. With aggressive negative caching, the validator also checks whether any cached and validated NSEC record denies the sought record. It does not answer this way when the incoming query has the CD bit set.

A validator will need an ordered data structure of NSEC and NSEC3 records for each signer domain name, called NSEC_TABLE in the text, to find covering records efficiently. If anything goes wrong in the algorithm, the resolver MUST resolve the query as usual, as though it did not implement the technique.

Appendix B gives a procedure to tell a nonexistent name from an empty non-terminal using NSEC: discard records that are not verified secure, do not cover the name, or come from a parent zone. If the surviving record's next name is a subdomain of the queried name, the name is an empty non-terminal; otherwise it is NXDOMAIN.
sections.eli5: The resolver keeps its notes sorted so it can quickly find the right one, and if anything looks odd it just asks the server like before.
